item.title: The Subtle Play Behind Generative AI’s Long Answers
item.description: Why longer answers may be about more than just being helpful.
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever asked Claude or ChatGPT a question and found yourself reading long answers? What if that is intentional - to drive engagement - to keep you on the app.

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

For technology companies, claiming and keeping customer attention - and turning it into revenue - is a subtle play. Social media companies like Meta and TikTok mastered it by bringing social interaction online and layering an advertising model on top. Users returned because their friends were there, notifications pulled them back, and eventually the feed itself became the habit. The more they used the platforms, the more data these companies accumulated, making advertising increasingly targeted.

Generative AI answers are deliberately long prose and not bulleted.

  1. When you read long text, you invariably spend more time on the app (the source) which are key KPIs on investor decks for why these companies continue to get funding.

  2. Long text has more context that can go wrong (the trigger) It gets interesting - long text brings in more context from saved memory or external sources and it may not serve the user need. As a result, it is triggers the user to respond.

  3. User response is logged and acts as reinforcement loop for the AI to learn about the user and update its model on how it should respond when it faces a similar question.


It’s useful context for when you find yourself skimming AI text and upping your reading speed.

item.title: To A/B or not to A/B?
item.description: Practical guide on choosing the right A/B test
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
The textbook A/B test is simple. Split users 50/50. Ship to one half. Measure the difference. Pick a winner.

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Across twelve years at Zynga, Instagram, Postmates, TikTok Shop, and Bilt, the single most expensive mistake I’ve watched data teams make is picking the wrong type of test. Here are the eight designs I actually reach for, and when to pick them

1. Standard A/B (User-Level Randomization)

Split users randomly. One bucket sees the new thing, one sees the old. Compare.

Works when: Users are independent. What test users do, doesn’t affect control users

Instagram Notes: Testing ranking logic for which Notes to surface in the inbox. My Note doesn’t affect whether you post one - at least not over a two-week window. Clean split, clean read.

Trap: People default here even when independence is violated (think SUTVA violation at Uber where discounted treatment users steal more supply affecting control users)

2. Cluster-Randomized (Geo / Market Splits)

Randomize groups - cities, regions, merchants - not users

Works when: Users inside a group interact with each other.

Postmates courier pricing: Flip courier pay for half of SF couriers, and the other half feel it too: same demand, same competition. The clean read is to flip all of SF and compare against a similar geo (e.g. Seattle). You trade statistical power for a real answer.

Trap: Geos aren’t interchangeable. San Francisco is not Phoenix. Match carefully.

3. Switchback Tests

Randomize based on time windows and not user. 30 minutes treatment, 30 minutes control, repeat for weeks.

Works when: Marketplaces, where supply and demand interact in real time (e.g. Uber, Postmates, Doordash)

Postmates dispatch: A new courier-matching algorithm can’t be user-split - if treatment couriers are faster, they steal orders that control couriers would have gotten. Treatment “wins” by cannibalizing control (!!). Switchbacks run city-wide, alternating windows. Each window is a quasi-independent observation.

Trap: Time-of-day, day-of-week, weather. Randomize windows carefully.

4. Marketplace / Supply-Side Tests

Randomize the supply (sellers, listings, drivers, creators) instead of users

Works when: Supply is finite and what you’re testing affects who sees what.

TikTok Shop: A naive user-level test on Shop ranking breaks SUTVA hard. Treatment users buy hot products → inventory runs out → control users see a different shelf. Treatment also consumes inventory control would’ve bought. Fix: randomize at the listing level, measure outcomes on listings. This was the core of the marketplace-aware testing framework I built there.

Trap: Listings still compete in the same search results. You often need supply-side splits and a switchback wrapper.

5. Diff-in-Diff / Synthetic Control

You can’t randomize. Compare the trend in the affected group against a similar unaffected group.

Works when: Geographic rollouts, regulatory changes, anything where reality blocks a clean experiment.

Bilt: New partner categories or benefits launched market-by-market, tied to the partner’s footprint. No clean A/B available. Diff-in-diff against matched markets - similar member density, similar pre-period spend - gave a defensible read. Synthetic control (a weighted basket of real markets used as a fake control) was the next step up when no single market matched well enough.

Trap: Parallel trends. If treatment and control were already diverging pre-launch, the estimate is garbage. Always plot the pre-period.

6. Holdout Tests

Hold 1-5% of users out from everything for months. Measure cumulative impact.

Works when: Every individual experiment “wins” but the topline isn’t moving. Or when you need long-term effects beyond a 2-week window.

Instagram Notes: Short-term tests showed engagement lifts. The real question at 0-to-100M scale was: does Notes move retention at week 8, or only engagement at day 3? Engagement and retention can diverge - a feature can be sticky short-term and net-negative on long-run retention. You’d never know without a holdout.

Trap: Holdouts are expensive, and there’s constant pressure to release them early. That destroys the measurement.

7. Interleaving (Ranking)

Interleave items from two rankers in the same feed for the same user. Measure which ranker’s items win engagement.

Works when: Search, feed, recs. >10x more sensitive than user-level A/B because each user is their own control.

Search and feed ranking: When comparing two ranking models, interleaving is the right first move before committing to a full A/B. You strip out the variance from “some users just engage more” and directly compare items.

Trap: Interleaving tells you which ranker is preferred. It doesn’t tell you whether shipping it moves the topline. Use it to triage candidates, then A/B the winner.

8. Multi-Armed Bandits

Dynamically shift traffic toward whichever arm is winning. You care about being directionally “right”

Works when: Care about the right decision on time >> clean measurement. (e.g. Push ad copy, headlines, creatives)

Push notifications: With 12 push variants with different “message copy” and finite budget, a fixed split wastes 11/12 of sends on losers. A bandit funnels traffic to winners, as evidence accrues. You ship faster, but you lose the clean unbiased effect size.

Trap: Bandits aren’t good at significance testing. It doesn’t answer “by how much did CTR lift?” cleanly

The Decision Frame

  1. Are users independent? If no - cluster, switchback, or supply-side.

  2. Can you randomize at all? If no - diff-in-diff or synthetic control.

  3. What are you trying to learn? Decision (bandit), preference (interleaving), short-term effect (A/B), long-term effect (holdout).

The test you pick is the answer you get.

If you’ve come across problems where the right test wasn’t obvious, reply or drop a comment.

item.title: Goals & North Star Metrics: A Content Recommendations Deep Dive
item.description: KPIs for Consumer Features: A Framework
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
Every experiment begins with a hypothesis. Using a streaming service’s content recommendations as an example, I dive deep into goals and metrics. Bad metrics cost months of engineering time and wrong decisions

Goal Framing

It has the following concepts:

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

  1. What feature is being tested?

  2. Which user is it for?

  3. What user behavior is being changed?

  4. When do we know when we have achieved success?

A good hypothesis answers four questions:

“By introducing a new recommendation row on the homepage [feature], we will help long-tenured users [user] discover new titles [user behavior being changed], measured by a sustained lift in 2-minute play rate [success metric] from that row without a corresponding drop in overall session conversion”

Metrics

North Star Metric (NSM)

  1. The NSM should be directly moved by the treatment of the experiment.

  2. The NSM is 2-minute play rate from the new row - not a raw click or hover, but a play that sustains long enough (i.e 2 mins) to signal genuine interest.

  3. This filters out misclicks that don’t convert to actual intent.

Guardrail Metrics

Guardrails are metrics that we keep constant while we move the northstar metric.

Two guardrails matter here.

  1. Overall session-to-play conversion - if the new row displaces a high-signal existing row, aggregate engagement could fall even as the new row’s own numbers grow.

  2. Retention and time spent - does the experiment affect subscription renewal or churn in the weeks following? Are users spending more time on the app and coming back for more sessions in the treatment group?

Secondary Metrics

These are metrics that offer us leading signals or verify directionally to confirm that we have moved in the right direction

  1. Hover rate and scroll-past rate act as leading signals - they tell you whether the row is earning attention before play events even fire.

  2. Series re-engagement rate (did the user return to that title in a subsequent session?) tells you whether the recommendation actually landed or was a one-and-done curiosity click.

Ecosystem Considerations

The biggest risk is cannibalization. A new row doesn’t create screen real estate - it displaces something.

If the lift in the new row’s play rate is fully offset by a drop in adjacent rows, the net value is zero. Segment the results by user tenure and content type: mid-tenure users with large taste profiles are the target users.

If the row mostly surfaces popular titles to new users, it's not discovering anything - it's just a bestseller list.

item.title: ChatGPT Plus vs Claude Pro: Why I switched?
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
Two products. Same price. One is trying to keep you engaged. The other is trying to get you out of the chat faster. I start with facts, look at human criteria and end with an opinion.

The Facts

  1. Context window: Claude 200K vs ChatGPT 128K - Claude wins

  2. Persistent memory: Claude’s memory is user-visible ChatGPT’s memory is more deeply integrated, more contextual - ChatGPT wins

  3. File uploads: ChatGPT handles docs and PDFs more reliably - ChatGPT wins

  4. Response length: ChatGPT is padded and recap-heavy; Claude is concise - Claude wins

  5. Refusals: Claude engages on nuance, explains boundaries. ChatGPT has more corp-speak standardized safety responses given its mass-y audience - Draw

  6. Web search: Both have it; ChatGPT’s is more mature and better cited - ChatGPT wins

  7. Coding: ChatGPT executes code in-chat. Claude excels at reasoning - Draw

  8. Multimodal ecosystem: ChatGPT has voice, image gen, data analysis; Claude has none - ChatGPT wins

  9. Hallucination honesty: Claude admits uncertainty; ChatGPT fabricates more, keeps bad news away - Claude wins

  10. Pricing: Both $20/month - Draw

The “Human” Criteria

  1. The “feel” of talking to it - Claude pushes back, disagrees, has opinions. ChatGPT tends to agree with you and tell you what you want to hear. That’s a huge daily-use difference that doesn’t fit neatly into “quality.”

  2. Does it actually follow your instructions? - You said write it in 3 bullet points, it gave you 7 lengthy paragraphs. You said be concise, it wrote an essay. Instruction-following is its own paradigm.

  3. Consistency - Run the same prompt twice. If this were an experiment, variance matters as much as the mean.

  4. Memory - Does it remember what you told it last Tuesday?

  5. When it says no - Both models refuse things, but how and when they do it feels very different. One feels like a cautious lawyer, one feels like a curious colleague who occasionally hits a wall. Worth naming.

  6. Speed on a bad day - Not peak performance, but what’s the experience at 2pm on a Tuesday when everyone’s using it?

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The Opinion

After the criteria and facts, here’s what I keep coming back to: these two products feel built around different incentives.

ChatGPT behaves like a friendly consumer-scale platform. Answers are long, thorough and optimized for time spent which is important for retention. Tone skews agreeable to offer a much needed “kick” - the same dopamine loop that keeps you scrolling on Facebook and Instagram.. Treading on questions with nuance, safety is prioritized. With over 800 Million users, engagement is key.

Claude feels built for a different environment. The tone is tighter and precise. It signals uncertainty more easily and pushes back more often with shorter responses. It feels designed for people who care about output quality over conversational comfort.

Consumer-scale products tend to optimize for time spent and retention.
Enterprise-oriented tools tend to optimize for precision and correctness.

At $20/month, they are playing distinctly different games.
You’re choosing the right collaborator.

I know my choice.

item.title: You’re Prompting LLMs Wrong: The Role Design Playbook
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
Great LLM output comes from role design. Every interaction is interpreted through three layers - system, user, and assistant - and each layer serving a different purpose.

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Let’s break this down.

System: who the model is

Definition
The system role defines the model’s identity.
Anything placed here is assumed to be always true, across every request.

Think of system as the bot’s job description plus house rules.

Common system role configurations

  1. Identity-only

    “You are a sentiment analysis bot.”

  2. Identity + hard constraints

    • What to prioritize

    • What to never do

  3. Identity + rubric

    • Clear definitions

    • Explicit weighting rules

Avoid putting task-specific input here. This is strictly persona.

System: Example

System:
You are a strict sentiment rater for public comments.
Output only an integer from 1–5.
1 = strongly negative, 3 = neutral, 5 = strongly positive.
If praise is followed by a serious complaint, prioritize the complaint.

At this point, the model knows who it is - without instructions on specific tasks or examples of response.

User: what the model should do right now

Definition
The user role supplies the current task and input.
It should be clean and to-the-point.

If you find yourself repeating rules in user prompts, those rules should be in the system (think of this as tactical while System is more strategic)

Common user role configurations

  1. Task-only input (Just the instruction + data)

    Classify the severity of this comment:
    “People like you are why Reels is trash 💀”

  2. Task + light constraints (Useful for one offs)

    Classify the severity (S0–S4) of this comment. Focus on harmful content not sarcastic humor.
    “People like you are why Reels is trash 💀”

User: Example

User:
Rate the sentiment (1–5) for the following comment:
“it was a great vibe but the food isn’t good”

On its own, models will overweight “great vibe” and return 4.

That’s where the assistant role comes in.

Assistant: how the model learns judgment

Definition
The assistant role establishes precedent.
It teaches the model how to think by example, not instruction.

This is where you encode nuance and expected output.

Assistant: Example

Assistant:
Comment: “Loved the decor, but the service was rude.” → 2
Comment: “Great vibe but the food isn’t good.” → 1
Comment: “Not bad. Not great. Fine.” → 3
Comment: “Best meal of my life. Coming back tomorrow.” → 5

The model now scores complaints over praise

Putting it together

With:

  • System defining identity

  • Assistant defining output via examples

  • User supplying input

item.title: How I use ChatGPT?
item.description: A practical guide to configuring ChatGPT
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
From drafting copy at work, to writing code, to even thinking through life decisions, AI chatbots are everywhere now. After using ChatGPT almost daily for a long time, I realized something important: results depend far less on clever prompts and far more on how you set the system up for success.

This piece documents the few things that consistently worked for me. None of this is theoretical. It’s just what reduced noise, sped things up, and made the outputs usable.

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

I break my approach into four parts.

I’ve subdivided my approach into the following sections

  1. Custom Instructions: Instructions that work across chats

  2. Characteristics: The personality of your chatbot that can range from enthusiastic and personable to professional and direct

  3. Project Instructions: Use-case defined folder to reference chats, with a private only option

  4. Prompting: A back and forth exchange with the Chatbot

Custom Instructions

Rules that apply across every chat

This is the place where you put in instructions to how the app should respond to your every prompt on every chat. Given the instructions of keeping it brief, the bot usually responds in a “no fluff” manner. Think of this as your default operating system

Characteristics

The personality of the chatbot

This is different from rules. Characteristics are about tone.

Some people like enthusiastic, friendly responses. I don’t. I prefer direct, neutral, sometimes even blunt replies - closer to how I’d want a senior coworker to answer a question.

Setting this explicitly helps avoid the overly polite, over-explained style that wastes reading time.

Project Instructions

Projects are underrated.

I use them to organize verticals of my life - Data Science, Wellbeing, Writing, Immigration, etc. Each project has its own instructions that take precedence over global memory.

By default LLM outputs are more and more verbose, increasing reading time - this overhead can be avoided by “project instructions” where in my case I explicitly state to reduce it to 5 bullets each time and ask a relevant follow up so my response prompting can be a monosyllabic yes or a no - very efficient in practice.

There’s another benefit: projects can be made private. That’s useful when working with sensitive or personal information that you don’t want bleeding into other contexts.

Prompting

Constraints > cleverness

Prompting is mostly about constraints and tone.

Prompting can be optimized by creating constraints and the tonality of your message. A recent study suggested 4% better LLM results with “rude” prompts when compared to “polite prompts” which nudges the understanding that pushing your Chatbot may help it get to the specific answer quicker.

In summary things that helped in prompting —

  1. Be explicit about structure: Answer <specific to this topic> with <5 bullets> and try to be as <exhaustive> as possible with mutually <exclusive> bullets and offer <one key recommendation>

  2. Start new chats All LLM output is unsupervised which in layman terms is that it can be “different each time” and at least one output may be totally random or out of cue. The longer the chats, the more context it has to converge on and the more mistake it can make to be precise to the “question” at hand. Therefore, start new chats (even possibly referencing the prior chat for context), the speediness of response and specificity both spike in my experience.

  3. Treat it like a tool, not a person Anthropomorphizing ChatGPT as “your best friend” feels natural, but it slows things down. Direct prompts get direct answers.

In Summary

Most improvements don’t come from better prompts. They come from configuration.

Once you:

  • lock in brevity,

  • control tone,

  • isolate context,

  • and enforce structure,

the chatbot becomes faster, quieter, and useful.

More in Part 2.

item.title: Product Case Study 101: A 4 step approach
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
Data Scientists on consumer products are often asked “Daily Active Users are down, can you investigate why?” or “Logins are down” - I am going to lay out the most simple framework to tackle the “how”

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

  1. Clarify “Context”

    1. What is the Metric? (e.g. Minutes / user)

    2. What is the Product? (e.g. Instagram Stories)

    3. Who’s the User? (e.g. Power users, Users in Brazil)

    4. What’s the time period? (e.g. week over week decline)

  2. “Frame” the problem: With clarified context, we can frame it as 

“We are seeing minutes / user going down on Instagram’s Stories Product where we see a week over week decline ”

  1. Analyze in layers (Go from low effort cuts → High effort cuts)

    1. Temporal (time): Was there an unusual spike for the metric the prior week? Did we see the same spike this time last year? Is the metric below the baseline established?

    2. Data integrity: Do we have completeness and accuracy of data that is supplying the dashboards that sees this decline?

    3. Tech outages: Was there any tech related failures this week? Is the decrease on any specific app version, split by iOS vs Android?

    4. Check metric adjacencies: Likely that when minutes per user goes down, other metrics may also see a decrease, like stories sessions per user?

    5. User segments: Is this isolated to a customer segment? Do power users (i.e who use the product more see a more pronounced effect?

    6. Geo segments: Is this isolated to a specific country where we are testing a new feature that may have regressed this metric?

    7. Can we tie it to a feature or event: Can we see this regression on an A/B test on Stories product? Can we tie it to a marketing event?

  2. Tell a story not just data points A good investigation is not just analysis - it’s storytelling.

    1. What happened (the decline, quantified).

    2. Where did it happen (specific user/product segments).

    3. Why did it happen (root cause hypotheses, evidence).

    4. What to do next (recommend rollback, deeper analysis, or monitoring).

  1. Final Takeaways

    1. Always clarify context: Avoid the chase without context ; Persuasively ask “whys” consecutively

    2. Go from most likely least effort → high effort ; exercise product and common sense

    3. Slice segments → Ratios and average hide the story (ratios can be high at launch given denominator base is small before the metric scales and law of averages catches up)

    4. Tie to product, business and marketing events: Usually with a product launch (moving users to a different consumption surface we can cannibalize the original surface), or with a marketing push, we can drive unusual seasonality that will regress the following week.

    5. Communicate succinctly: Optimize for reading time, with executive summary at top and a long appendix for the reader that dives into details.

Source: TechRadar

item.title: Data Science Playbook Part 4 - Rent Neighborhood Rewards
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
The Premise

When I joined Rent Rewards as the fourth data hire, I stepped into a company trying to turn rent → into a rewards ecosystem locally in a neighborhood premised by the fact a large XX% share of consumer wallet took place within 5 miles of where a person lived.

My role quickly expanded to supporting data for two pods → Dining and Payments, while also supporting our Customer Success team. That meant one week I’d be debugging why a rent payment failed, and the next I’d be supporting analytics on dining partnerships that could drive incremental GMV.

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Scaling Customer Success with Data

Early on, much of my impact came from analytics for operations. We had recurring issues across rent payments, loyalty points, and customer support escalations. Instead of chasing each problem, I built frameworks to:

  • Identify the root cause of recurring issues.

  • Quantify their impact on loyalty and churn.

  • Prioritize engineering fixes with a data-backed case.

This shifted CS from a reactive function into a data-informed partner to product.

Reimagining Dining as a Growth Pod

Dining was where Rent Rewards could move from “just a rent card” to an everyday lifestyle product grounded in the “neighborhood”. We experimented with multiple engagement levers:

  • Exclusive partnerships in neighborhoods where Rent Rewards was the “only” accepted payment method.

  • Mobile checkout in restaurants through the Rent Rewards app.

  • Split pay and guest pay, making it easy for members to bring friends into the ecosystem.

  • House accounts where Rent Rewardsstored balances for members and automatically debited at partner restaurants.

These weren’t just product features → they were experiments in behavioral design. Every transaction became an opportunity to close the loop between users, merchants, and rewards.

Merchant Dashboard

We didn’t just think about users: we built data pipelines and dashboards for merchants. Running semantic level dbt models, we surfaced insights on volume, repeat visits, and lift from Rent Rewards-exclusive offers. Merchants could log in and “see the value” of the partnership, and use targeted offers to target users “hyperlocally” that lived in the neighborhood. That transparency was key to scaling partnerships.

Ridesharing Promos: Cross selling partnerships

One of my favorite projects was quantifying Ride-sharing promos run through Rent Rewards. We discovered that XX% of renters who got into Rent Rewards rental Properties did not have a specific Ride sharing app (we had partnered with) in their wallet. That insight helped us position Rent Rewards not just as a rent rewards company, but as part of the everyday mobility driving stronger mindshare.

Lessons Learned

My time at Rent Rewards reinforced a few truths about scaling data science in early consumer products:

  1. CX helps you learn what’s wrong at a startup – Fixing customer support tickets helped me understand the core product failures that customers were facing (e.g. Merchant names on transactions on the Rent Rewards app did not name the merchant as we were the “merchant of record” )

  2. Ecosystems win when both sides see value – Building merchant dashboards and showing merchants “on a map” the targeted customer opportunity from neighborhood Rent Rewards properties meant more value in targeted promos.

  3. Non-obvious data creates leverage – Rent, dining, and rides may look unrelated, but tying them together created the flywheel.

Why This Matters

Rent Rewards proved that rewards aren’t just about points → its about neighborhood loyalty (building a local rewards ecosystem where the input is rent).

item.title: Data Science Playbook Pt 3 - Learnings at Postmates
item.description: Recaps learnings at food delivery app
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
The Background

Postmates was the first to pioneer a gig-economy based food delivery model, and was eventually surpassed by Tony Xu’s Doordash in marketshare, to be acquired by Uber after Uber’s efforts to acquire GrubHub fell through, and to claim Postmates’ youthful brand, its’ merchant network and the Los Angeles market, where Postmates’ had more than 50% marketshare.

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

I joined the Postmates’ Consumer Data Science team of three analysts, where we were given a free hand to figure out the key challenges to driving consumer retention, increase ordering behavior and grow basket size (also, known as average order value).

The Problem

We saw 3 hurdles for consumers as they navigated our app

  1. Selection - Did users like the merchants we had?

  2. Availability - Was this merchant available and would the delivery come in time?

  3. Price - Did the price meet user’s expectations?

Quickly, I figured that these 3 hurdles were the biggest hurdles to go over, with selection finding something you liked involved a decision paradox with more and more merchants, and more and more items. If you got through selection, users faced increasing price sensitivities to order a pizza at $14.99, and if they got through selection and availability, the merchant may not delivery on time or worse be closed affecting availability.

The Solution

The framing of the solution became

How do we convert all users, who have selection (find something they like? → Add to Cart), who have availability (merchant open and delivery within 30 mins) and at a price they like?

These users look like users at the Checkout Page - just before the order is placed.

I reckoned we should be converting 100% of users at checkout who have hurdled through selection, availability, price.

What were the key reasons Checkout users dropped off?

  1. Pricing at checkout (e.g Merchant fee, Delivery fee, Service fee)

  2. Address issues

  3. Miscellaneous (e.g. Changed their mind)

What were the key reasons pricing led to dropoff for Checkout customers?

  1. Built a classification model to predict the “relative” and “directional impact” of lowered merchant fees, lowered delivery fees and lowered platform service fees to figure out which fee played a role at price sensitivities at checkout

  2. Concluded that reducing delivery fees made the most gain on user checkout

  3. Rolled out A/B tests to test free delivery for new users in the LA market, given demand was consistent

  4. Led to an X% uptick in new users placing their first order on Postmates’ in the Los Angeles market

  5. First orders led to 65% second orders and 35% third orders, that generated more revenue for the platform.

Retention = Growth and thereby by understanding the context of “why” users at checkout didn’t convert (e.g. Pricing) and solving for it based on the parameters that had the most sensitivity (e.g. Delivery fee over other fees), we were able to get the first orders in for X% more users, who we retained and generated more lifetime revenue offsetting for their acquisition costs.

item.title: Data Science Playbook Pt 2 - Learnings at TikTok
item.description: Recaps learnings at TikTok Shop and going from 0 to $XX GMV
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
China has an involution culture shaped by 9-9-6, which is that you eat, breathe and sleep as breaks - while you work 9 am - 9 pm, 6 days a week. Bytedance, TikTok’s parent company entered the US market with the acquisition of a startup called musical.ly, and then grew to replicate Douyin (the name of the Chinese TikTok app) to scale and find mass adoption in the US market. While the US market is makes roughly 50-80% of the revenue of any international consumer app that is ad-driven, China makes roughly 80% of overall TikTok revenue, in broadstrokes.

Background
After my stint on launching Notes at Instagram, I moved over to TikTok, 3 months prior to the E-commerce launch. While most tech companies in the US operate in a pod structure with design, data, product and engineering, the set up for TikTok Shop was different. It was an operations-driven company, looking to blueprint its’ success framework in Asia and bring it to the US market with minimal changes. The Operation leader (let’s called them X), was insistent on using the same rubric to find creators who would sell products with the same enthusiasm as live creators in China, sold products on Douyin. At Meta, bug identification to solution took around 1-2 days, when launching a feature, at TikTok, bugs were identified and neutralized within hours. There was a ton of velocity and eagerness on launching commerce and while TikTok’s revenue so far was ad-monetized revenue, there was increasing appetite for using a closed loop model (User sees a product → User buys a product fulfilled by TikTok Shop) vs open-loop (User sees a product → User clicks ad) and semi closed loop (User sees a product → User buys a product fulfilled by third party). Owning the entire experience meant that we had to build trust early as users tend to buy low-priced items (commodity items) first before trusting a platform to buy a TV, Microwave. The stage was set.

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

My role

I spent my initial few months on the Recommendation team where we assessed the number of commerce videos we could show on Short form video controlling for churn. Next, as someone who could access US user data at a granular level (which my Chinese colleagues couldn’t), we had to figure out the following

  1. Where do we place the Shop tab with minimal disruption to organic traffic?

  2. What products do feature first to our users?

  3. Do we feature products with higher quality / high cost vs lower quality / low cost?

  4. How do we acquire the right products, incubate them and grow them to be “hero products” such that there is reliability of revenue?

In the first few months, we hustled our way to the first question - understanding that we were displacing XX% of traffic that was flowing in from the iconic For You Page (FYP) to the Friends tab, while Friending was Meta’s core competency (Entertainment being TikTok’s) , it was something that TikTok was playing catchup to (as Meta did for Short Form video). Once we figured that out, there were 3 areas where commerce was served up - LIVE, Short Form Video and Shop Tab (the tab we replaced the Friends tab with, that looked exactly like Amazon’s home page).

For the next few months, I spent an inordinate amount of time working with a Senior Director (who was locally based, and spoke english → both being rarities in TikTok at the time - where I found myself lucky), to work on a strategy for the following.

  1. How do we acquire the right products across industry verticals like Fashion, Beauty, Healthcare, Furniture, etc?

  2. How do we in Minimum Viable way, figure out which products drove the highest traction to “incubate” them?

  3. How do we ensure a Pareto with 80% of our revenue insured by stable “hero” products that customers kept buying over time?

Trading off between $ and Order

For this we had two metrics - GPM and OPM - GPM referred to Gross Merchandise Volume that we generated for 1000 impressions of a product and OPM referred to as Orders we generated for 1000 impressions of a product. Initially, to drive transaction frequency (or, in other words to get the user to buy more products → we focused on driving purchases of low priced products that would drive more mindshare while the long tail of users would finally buy furniture → a model that TEMU and other marketplaces also do).

Product exposure in exchange for price-match

Then, we boosted products for sellers who would help reduce the prices for us to be competitive with Amazon, TEMU in exchange for traffic. We were in the business of trading off eyeballs in exchange for ad revenue, GMV sales through product, and in this case sellers helped match the lowest price on the market for more and more exposure. By now, we had scaled GMV ground up from $0 to $XXM, in less than 4 months. I continued to advise the various business teams on (1) Price ($0-$10 vs $20-$30) , (2) Category (e.g. Furniture vs Sport) and (3) Industry (e.g. Home vs Fashion). Although Collectibles (e.g. trading cards) generated high user repeat purchases, high average order value, we deprioritized it since we had to go for on-brand categories like Fashion. There were competitive landscape considerations, given startups like Whatnot primarily drove the Collectibles (trading cards, pokémon cards) marketshare through live (a perishable card reveal use case that generates engagement through principle of scarcity - a “shiny” card that drives intrigue and therefore, sales. With TikTok Shop, the idea was to be a trendy marketplace that would capitalize on the trends that emerged from organic engagement - Fashion was on point.

Causal link between reviews driving sales

Lastly, I moved to the User Product Reviews team where the objective was to (1) Grow user reviews (2) understand the causal link between user reviews → sales. My correlative studies so far showed that it was difficult to link sales to reviews on the app - products with reviews had to have sales and therefore the two were related but I quickly wanted to establish a causal link by running a test where hid the star rating altogether to see the impact on conversion. We had seen earlier that given the price was low, conversion rate would inflect even at moderate/ low avg rating - meaning that it was entirely possible for a product with 3.5 rating to have high sales, given the price was <$10.

In addition to this, the advent of AI took over, and we had to fast follow with AI Insights (e.g. tags that summarized wisdom of crowds from reviews such as “T-shirt fits well”) and AI Summaries (long prose version of Insights), that were already mature in places like Amazon and were building perception for what a user might expect off reviews. However, the number of users scrolling and seeing detailed reviews were very low and we had to incentivize - (a) users adding more reviews after purchases (b) users seeing detailed reviews to create an appetite for these AI products. All this while, we hadn’t talked about whether the sentiment of a review would actually lead to a proclivity of user to purchase a product, on a marketplace highly weighted by price, promotion and discounting.

While this is a brief overview, watch out for Part 3 where I will discuss more on product analytics / data science journeys at consumer tech.

Please read Part 1: Instagram and Zynga for my learnings there

item.title: Data Science Playbook Pt 1 - Learnings at Instagram & Zynga
item.description: Recaps learnings at Instagram and Zynga
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
My career spans a number of marketplaces - gaming, social media, e-commerce. This article is an attempt to distill my key takeaways at each of the places I worked at.

Part 1 consists Zynga and Instagram.

Watch out for bulleted Playbook learnings after each section.

Instagram

Instagram was a very design-led company when I joined. For a company that made almost half the revenue of Meta (the parent company), it had surprisingly low personnel to support. For instance, FB Stories (borrowed from Instagram Stories) had 6 Data Scientists for every Data Scientist that was on Instagram Stories. So the level of responsibility here was high and more focussed.

My first assignment on the team was to join the Sharing org - responsible for Stories, Feed and Reels - 3 top sharing formats on Instagram. I was excited by the challenges that lay ahead- the first of which was to ship “Add Yours” - a way to collaboratively add-on to your friend’s coffee photo by picking a coffee photo from your own gallery. It tackled 3 core principles of engagement - social proof, mimicry and users needing inspiration or a cue to sharing (a friend’s photo gave them the cue and adding on to a thread reduced the barrier to share). It engaged people to the extent that some of these threads ran into Millions of photos being shared, one for
”plant a tree for every share” that would run into legal challenges. After that viral launch I was handed, Instagram Notes (which was called “Status” then). Situation was that “sending a one-way text message” was the key signal why teens would choose Instagram over Snapchat or vice versa and we had to design a feature that allowed people to create Notes, share them with close friends and invite first time messages. The only caveat was that it was a particularly difficult to get people to send messages if they hadn’t before.

Among things that we had to navigate included

  • (a) audience that was not large to become “broadcast-y” and not too small that would affect cold start

  • (b) Design X vs Design Y: One Featuring author over note vs Note over author affected if people wanted to read any note from a close friend or just a note that they could read better even from someone in their outer social circles

  • (c) making the messaging tab a content consumption surface (not ad monetized and trading off against revenue),

  • (d) displacing “active now” friends that occupied spot,

  • (e) adding “Music notes” (!) - pardon the pun, and believing that it would somehow scale and work.

    At this time, I created a decision tree with series of “country tests” that we would run for soft launches before our key launch in US where majority of our revenue came from - we also had tease out the revenue loss that would come from users navigating to this surface. I was well supported by the Director of Product, Design, UX Research and my data org as I designed the series of tests that would help narrow (a) through (e), and communicating detail to engineers on detail (read: character limits of notes for optimal engagement, localization challenges in Arabic vs Korean vs English and to succinctly communicate tests results to leadership, guiding towards the launch to 1B users - and Instagram’s 4th new sharing format, that on an entirely different surface - (not Home) but Messages and enabled 1B IG users to more easily access close friends through 1 way messages they had never sent before, all because they had Close Friends’ Note as a “cue”.

Key playbook learnings →

  • Concise Choices. Be succinct—limit to two options—when seeking leadership feedback, and stay detail‑oriented / rigorous with the engineering team.

  • Bundle Bets and Align early with Stakeholders. Prioritize and bundle multiple parameters into a single variant instead of running N + tests; this quickly narrows choices and early alignment sets expectations

  • Frame for Learning. Use “Pros & Cons” / “Learning” tests rather than “Elimination” tests when aligning large orgs and core features.

  • Test Through Ambiguity. Keep the bar to test low and ship high; when ad‑revenue sensitivity looked low in India and Brazil, we validated in Europe to generalize findings.

Zynga

At Zynga, I supported analytics for one of the company’s largest franchises - FarmVille 2. Back in the day, during Zynga onboarding, the team’s first assignment was simple: Play FarmVille until I hit level 20. That deep dive was formative in uncovering bugs and building empathy for the product you can’t find on a dashboard. Solutions begin in "experience".

I learned about virtual economies and Japanese Gacha “treasure chests” (“loot‑box”) that let you trade off effort in the game in exchange for payment through currency. There are two types of currency - primary (that you get in the Millions and spend in the Millions to drive spending behavior - these are gold coins in most cases and a secondary currency that is limited < 100 usually for most players that people spend actual money $$ to acquire. The secondary currency often can be exchanged for millions of gold coins (our primary currency). This drives the basic abstraction - a currency you earn and spend easily and another that is expensive to acquire that can be exchanged for the primary currency. There are loops of all sorts to get you to do a series of actions and trade off effort for currency (or paying). Games build new features to create new repetitive loops that are engaging at first, then become difficult and allow 2-step currency models to let you buy yourself some “progress”. This is at the core of gaming, when the loops don’t drive curiosity and “near win-near loss” situations - where the player felt that he could win the next time, the game usually dies. This is at the heart of engagement - keeping it “just interesting” but never going overboard.

Key playbook learnings →

  • Embed yourself in the loop. Playing to level 20 surfaced hidden bugs and built empathy dashboards can’t.

  • Two‑tier economy powers monetization. A plentiful primary currency & scarce premium currency let players trade effort for $$ while still feeling meaningful progress.

  • Sustain “near‑win” tension. Design loops where the player is always one step from success; too easy or too hard breaks engagement.

  • Refresh loops frequently. Introducing new features resets curiosity and gives veterans fresh progression paths.

  • Guard against currency inflation. Tune exchange rates so premium currency stays valuable without tipping into pay‑to‑win territory.

Read Data Science Playbook Pt 2 - Learnings at TikTok here and Part 3: Postmates here

item.title: Core Pillars to Social Gaming
item.description: Primer on how games use tactics to drive growth
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
29

Ever wondered what makes Social games tick? What creates the habits that drive players to return to games like Farmville 2 and Candy Crush among others. As Nir Eyal put it in his book “Hooked”, such habits are created by driving user motivation, giving the user an ability to action and facilitating repeatable behavior through triggers.

My experiences in gaming has led me to formalize the pillars on which this is based. They apply to any consumer app that creates user habits. I borrow from Lewis C Lin’s Decode and Conquer and my wonderful peers in the companies I’ve worked at to articulate this.

  1. Data Loop: The adage here is that the more user information that you store on your games the stickier your users will get. With games, this means game progression (XP points)and feature progress (X events played daily). When we design features for our games, we need to map roughly 80% of the journey in roughly half the projected engagement minutes to drive early user engagement. The feeling of early accomplishment drives player motivation towards the end despite the journey getting exponentially tougher (final 20% in the 50% time). Also, this is exactly the sweet spot where F2P games monetize since players already feel invested. Consider, Pokemon Go the journey of leveling from 1 to 40 takes an exponential turn once the player reaches 30. The level 30 user is already well habituated in the data loop and will continue to invest game time.

  2. Compulsion Loop: The capitalist mind of the 21st century is already wired to doing things that bring in rewards. The Compulsion Loop facilitates such behavior by giving a user a bait to return every 4 hours or so. Modern games drive user sessions through treasure chests or loot boxes that unlock in a stipulated time period. These Chests & Loot boxes have one thing in common — The Japanese “Gacha” mechanic. The Gacha provides the user a randomized reward for every unlock — building in an element of surprise. Users log in every 4 hours to find out what their loot boxes have in store. The element of surprise builds a habit that players cannot forego long after they’ve realized an approximate value of chests upon multiple iterations of opening loot boxes.

  3. Social Loop: The Pareto principle reads that 80% of the monetary value comes from 20% of the users. So how do Free-to-Play games leverage the 80% of their user base who don’t monetize? Well the answer is social value. Each player has the ability to send viral feeds that bring in other players. Conversely, when a player churns, there is a direct ripple on his/her social circle as an effect of his lost viral feeds.This is quantified in by K-factor i.e the number of viral feeds sent by a player multiplied by the conversion on them. Games leverage this by building mechanic of social tasking- For e.g. FarmVille 2 has a mechanic of adding neighbors to your farm and facilitating interaction through sending/receiving gifts through viral feeds on Facebook. Players could circumvent game tasks by posting on Newsfeed for gift items that brought other players into the game.

Stay tuned for more.

item.title: Free item Framework
item.description: Primer on designing free items in consumer tech apps to drive growth
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
Growth is retention — in every business and its’ no different for consumer internet apps. By retention, we refer to the return rate of customers within a certain period to the app to do a specific kind of action. It varies with different business models for instance, gaming companies want to get users to spend as much time on the app to maximize impressions for advertisements that it runs. On the other hand, food delivery apps expect a customer to return and order from the restaurant catalog it serves. To inculcate this behavior of recall to the app, companies adopt dozens of tactics, one of which involves providing the product that is sells for a discounted price. Games give away free loot boxes and food delivery companies give out free burgers on specific days to bait users to return and create long lasting habits. This is TAVI framework is to elucidate how such a free item drop may be realized.

It consists of 4 steps — Trigger, Action, Variable Reward and Investment

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Trigger

What gets the user to the product?

External triggers for the user includes the in-app push and message copy

Internal triggers for the user such as lunch/dinner hour peaks when the user inherently has a need to open the app

Action

The simplest action that a user takes in anticipation of the variable reward.

This includes

  1. Opening the app

  2. Viewing the item

  3. Clicking into the item page

  4. Adding and ordering the item

Variable Reward

The free item can variable based on the kind of restaurants offering the deal on any given day.

This is beneficial for two reasons:

  1. Does not lock the platform to the kind of items/restaurants needed for the drop. It can vary.

  2. Creates an element of surprise for the user hooking them

Investment

What is a bit of work to be done by the user in order to return to the app?

  1. Users that get the item have cues to return on a specific day/specific time

  2. Drops may be specific to times we want to drive app opens

  3. Users that do not get the free item is the larger base from whom the expectation of getting it the next time creates habits of return.

Reference: Nir Eyal Hooked [2014]

item.title: Growth = Retention
item.description: A primer on building retention analytics
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
Growth is retention. Most consumer internet companies do growth modeling in some form or another to slice and profile customers based on varying engagement levels and/or longevity of association with the product. This presents one of the many approaches that can be used to understand growth.

Definitions

Let’s cover some basic definitions before we jump into the specifics of the framework

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

  • Action This defines the specific action that users must do for them to count as retained e.g. Logging into an ad-driven business like Facebook or purchase a meal on an online food delivery marketplace like Postmates or DoorDash

  • Cycle This can be thought of as the maximum time frame in which you expect your average customer to perform the action. For e.g For a food delivery marketplace, you may expect your average customer to order delivery at least once a week (perhaps on the weekends)

Segments

The segments here are defined based on the frequency of action within the cycle and on when they were acquired (for new users).

  • Continuing Users Refers to the most loyal cohort for the product that performs the action at least once in a cycle. Small inflections here may be carefully monitored.

  • Returning Users Refers to the cohort that either has irregular purchasing patterns / switches to competition / etc. This cohort will see inflections with alternating weeks of activity where they perform the action once in 2 cycles.

  • New Users Refers to users that installed the app the prior week. As the cliché goes, early impressions matter and their second week retention may need close monitoring. For new users, the acquisition campaign and period of acquisition are additional factors to profile on.

  • Installs This refers to the users installs/signups that we had this week. We will measure retention rates for the three user cohorts above barring this one.

Retention Framework

We take a 3 business cycle horizon (or 21 days) from our observation point i.e. today. We can then calculate return rates as follows:

  • Continuing User Return Rate (CURR) This refers to the share of users who were active this week among continuing users i.e users active in week — 2 and week — 1

  • Returning User Return Rate (RURR) This refers to the share of users who were active this week among returning users i.e. users active in week — 2 and not in week — 1

  • New User Return Rate (NURR) This refers to the share of users who were active this week among new users i.e. users activated in week — 1

Exhibit showing the same in a tabular format

X = Active O = Inactive

Stitching it all together

In summary, lead up to a formula that encapsulates all our user segments to build up our weekly active user base.

Weekly Actives = (CURR * Continuing users) + (RURR * Returning users) + (NURR * New users) + Installs

We now have a framework to understand retention sliced by user segments that can refresh daily on a moving basis. Hope this was helpful

item.title: Experimentation heuristics to launch 0-1 social media products
item.description: How to launch a feature using country tests for a social media product
item.dc:creator: Dev Pal
item.content:encoded:
Context

The foundation of a social media app's success lies in organic products, pivotal for engaging users and boosting ad revenue. Embracing the "zero-to-one" philosophy, inspired by Peter Thiel, involves transitioning from conception of the feature to a full feature release.

Framing

In this example, we explore a "narrowcast" text-based sharing feature (think a micro-twitter) for close-friends to spark conversations, a balance between mass-engaging broadcast mediums and high-pressure direct messages on the app.

Thanks for reading Dev’s Newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

  • "Narrowcast" emphasizing small-group sharing among close friends, strikes a balance, fostering meaningful interactions triggered by shared cues, "Spiderman movie at 5?" (narrowcasted to 5 Close friends may act as cue to start conversations)

How may we test a "narrowcast" text-based sharing feature in the message tab that acts as cue to start conversations among "close friends"?

Goals

The Northstar metric focuses on increasing the share of daily active users sending at least one message daily. Guardrails, like ecosystem revenue and overall engagement, ensure stability while pursuing the Northstar.

  • Northstar metric is the share of users in daily active users who send at least one message everyday -> we aim to increase this

  • Guardrail are metrics that we want to keep constant/ mindful of while we move the north star, this may include ecosystem metrics such as revenue and engagement --> keep constant / not decrease

Additional components to test

  • Content-over-author vs Author-over-content designs emphasizes the delicate balance between prioritizing people or content in the user interface. (Do you observe the author and then content or vice versa?)

  • Audience models range from broad (All Followers) to narrow (Close Friends). Additional features, like Friends Active on the Message tab, aim to strike a balance between availability and content richness.

Test design

Country tests assess the feature's value before a full release, considering factors like insulation and messaging behavior, by limiting users in a country to have access to the feature.

Our country choice for testing depends on:

  • Insulation | what % of country interacts within the country itself (higher the insulation audience, the better to prevent leaks from testing period before full release)

  • Messaging | what % of users in country sends messages (there is a need to test in a country that has a base need for messaging to measure lift)

Producer-Consumer tests measure the feature's impact on ecosystem metrics, by keeping some users from producing / consuming the feature

  • In this test, the holdout group, excluded from experiencing the feature, cannot produce or consume it. This allows us to gauge the feature's impact on both the Northstar metric and overall ecosystem metrics, including time spent, engagement, and revenue.

  • The tradeoff, however, is that content from users on the test variant won't reach 100% of the audience (as they are coupled), as some users in the country won't see the feature at all. Despite this tradeoff, we prioritize understanding if the feature adds value to the ecosystem, striking a balance in our evaluation.

Test different markets

Testing across geographies acknowledges diverse user needs. No one-size-fits-all; some regions prioritize engagement with lower revenue, others focus on higher revenue but lower engagement.

Finding Nuance

  • Optimal character limits balance deep sharing and readability.

  • Balancing content visibility and author prominence impacts user engagement.

  • Localization considerations: Arabic (right to left) and Korean (efficient context in fewer characters) raise questions about language-specific character limits

Tradeoffs

With large social apps, launching a social feature, almost always trades off with existing activity on the app, it is important to meaningfully quantify the trade-off.

  • Making message a consumption surface Shifting users to the Messaging tab risks disrupting Home Tab engagement. Quantify potential losses in engagement or revenue for informed decision-making, especially considering the 6+ months scale-up period before monetization.

  • Cold start dynamics Starting with a larger audience aids feature distribution, while a smaller audience maintains nuanced sharing. Striking a balance between broad reach and nuanced goals is crucial for success.

Conclusion

This overview provides an initial overview into the heuristics of designing zero-to-one experiments in social media. By addressing core user needs and carefully testing features, the app aims to enhance engagement, drive meaningful conversations, and ultimately boost ad revenue.

The scope of this read covers some of the heuristics of designing a zero to one experiments for nascent social media features without discussing statistics.
